Abstract 
Despite strong performance of deep learning models in reMnal disease detecMon, most systems produce 
staMc predicMons without clinical reasoning or interacMve explanaMon. Recent advances in mulMmodal 
large language models (MLLMs) integrate diagnosMc predicMons with clinically meaningful dialogue to 
support clinical decision-making and paMent counseling. In this study, OcularChat, an MLLM, was ﬁne-
tuned from Qwen2.5-VL using simulated paMent-physician dialogues to diagnose age-related macular 
degeneraMon (AMD) through visual quesMon answering on color fundus photographs (CFPs). A total of 
705,850 simulated dialogues paired with 46,167 CFPs were generated to train OcularChat to idenMfy key 
AMD features and produce reasoned predicMons. OcularChat demonstrated strong classiﬁcaMon 
performance in AREDS, achieving accuracies of 0.954, 0.849, and 0.678 for the three diagnosMc tasks: 
advanced AMD, pigmentary abnormaliMes, and drusen size, signiﬁcantly outperforming exisMng MLLMs. 
On AREDS2, OcularChat remained the top-performing method on all tasks. Across three independent 
ophthalmologist graders, OcularChat achieved higher mean scores than a strong baseline model for 
advanced AMD (3.503 vs. 2.833), pigmentary abnormaliMes (3.272 vs. 2.828), drusen size (3.064 vs. 
2.433), and overall impression (2.978 vs. 2.464) on a 5-point clinical grading rubric. Beyond strong 
objecMve performance in AMD severity classiﬁcaMon, OcularChat demonstrated the ability to provide 
diagnosMc reasoning, clinically relevant explanaMons, and interacMve dialogue, with high performance in 
subjecMve ophthalmologist evaluaMon. These ﬁndings suggest that MLLMs may enable accurate, 
interpretable, and clinically useful image-based diagnosis and classiﬁcaMon of AMD.

Introduc+on 
Age-related macular degeneraMon (AMD) remains a leading cause of irreversible vision loss among older 
adults. It aﬀects nearly 200 million people worldwide, with numbers projected to increase with 
populaMon aging1. Clinically, AMD encompasses a spectrum of progressive macular changes, ranging 
from earlier ﬁndings, parMcularly drusen accumulaMon and pigmentary abnormaliMes, to advanced 
disease, speciﬁcally geographic atrophy and neovascular AMD2-4. Early idenMﬁcaMon of AMD features 
and accurate risk straMﬁcaMon are essenMal for paMent counseling, monitoring, and Mmely intervenMon. 
In clinical pracMce and screening, tradiMonal diagnosis relies on human expert interpretaMon of reMnal 
images within clinical context. However, this process is Mme-consuming, subject to inter-observer 
variability, and diﬃcult to scale across large populaMons. Timely idenMﬁcaMon and risk straMﬁcaMon of 
AMD therefore remain challenging, highlighMng the need for automated tools capable of idenMfying 
advanced disease and analyzing precursor features such as drusen characterisMcs and pigmentary 
abnormaliMes5. 
Automated methods, parMcularly those based on deep learning, have become increasingly central to 
medical image analysis6-8, and have demonstrated robust performance in ophthalmology, including the 
detecMon of diabeMc reMnopathy (DR)9-12, glaucoma13-16, cataract17-19, and AMD5, 20-24.  Many of these 
systems have achieved high diagnosMc accuracy for speciﬁc tasks. However, most operate as task-speciﬁc 
classiﬁers that produce categorical outputs without explanaMon and with limited transparency. In 
contrast, clinical interpretaMon of reMnal ﬁndings is inherently contextual and communicaMve: clinicians 
must explain imaging ﬁndings, address paMent quesMons, discuss prognosis and modiﬁable risk factors, 
and integrate imaging results into broader care decisions. 
Recent advances in mulMmodal large language models (MLLMs), which integrate both image and 
language processing capabiliMes25-27, have created new opportuniMes for clinical support. These models 


5 
 
can answer and explain quesMons. Such capabiliMes align closely with the communicaMve and 
interpreMve aspects of ophthalmic care, where eﬀecMve explanaMon of reMnal ﬁndings is central to 
paMent counseling and shared decision-making. Rather than funcMoning solely as automated classiﬁers, 
mulMmodal systems may support clinicians by enhancing interpretability, consistency, and eﬃciency in 
reMnal image assessment and communicaMon28-33. 
In this study, we developed and evaluated OcularChat, an MLLM speciﬁcally designed for AMD-related 
reMnal image assessment and clinically grounded dialogue. In contrast to convenMonal vision-language 
models (VLMs) that rely on contrasMve language-image pre-training (CLIP)-style pretraining28 or separate 
visual and language encoders30, OcularChat was ﬁne-tuned end-to-end from a pretrained Qwen2.5-VL 
model using reMnal images paired with simulated paMent-physician dialogues derived from the Age-
Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS). We assessed its performance on three clinically relevant tasks: 
idenMfying advanced AMD, categorizing drusen size, and detecMng pigmentary abnormaliMes. More 
importantly, we introduced a clinician-designed grading rubric and conducted human expert assessment 
to examine the quality of its explanaMons and conversaMonal responses and compared these outcomes 
with those of the reference model. 
By jointly integraMng image-based diagnosis with interpretable, dialogue-based outputs and clinician-
centered evaluaMon, this work advances beyond prior benchmarking studies of mulMmodal ophthalmic 
models toward a clinically oriented assessment framework34. As MLLMs begin to enter clinical pracMce, 
rigorous clinician-centered evaluaMon is essenMal to ensure not only accurate feature idenMﬁcaMon but 
also reliable diagnosMc reasoning and dialogue that are safe and trustworthy in clinical semngs.

Discussion 
In this study, OcularChat was developed as a mulMmodal system for reMnal image interpretaMon, 
including interacMve dialogue and reasoning. Across all diagnosMc tasks, it achieved higher performance 
than general-purpose VLMs, as well as a domain-speciﬁc model. AddiMonally, according to subjecMve 
assessment by ophthalmologists, it achieved higher raMngs for diagnosMc reasoning and clinical 
usefulness compared with the reference model.  
Most VLMs are pretrained on general-domain data, with limited exposure to ophthalmic images and 
terminology, which can restrict performance in detailed reMnal image interpretaMon. OcularChat 
incorporates ophthalmology-speciﬁc data and dialogue-based supervision to address this gap. It was 
adapted from a pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-32B) and trained using CFPs and syntheMc paMent-
physician dialogues derived from clinical informaMon in the AREDS dataset. 
External validaMon showed that OcularChat generalizes more consistently across tasks on external data. 
Across all tested models, we observed a notable reducMon in performance for detecMng advanced AMD 
in AREDS2. This decline likely reﬂects diﬀerences in disease appearance in the modern treatment era, in 
which neovascular AMD is managed with anM–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy and 
may present with subtle or absent features on CFP, in comparison to the ﬂorid appearance of untreated 
neovascular AMD at the Mme of AREDS. Nonetheless, OcularChat sMll maintained a high accuracy score. 
Most prior works have focused on developing deep learning-based classiﬁcaMon models that produce 
ﬁxed numeric outputs, such as DeepSeeNet5, which demonstrates strong predicMve performance but 
provides limited interpretability. More recent eﬀorts, including large mulMmodal ophthalmology dataset 


12 
 
(LMOD)34, evaluated VLMs for ophthalmic image understanding and diagnosis. While LMOD provides 
valuable insights into current VLMs’ capabiliMes, the results highlight substanMal limitaMons in 
ophthalmic image interpretaMon, parMcularly in clinically meaningful reasoning. In contrast, our work 
advances beyond benchmarking by developing an ophthalmology-speciﬁc VLM, with a focus on AMD-
related image assessment and explanatory conversaMonal output. 
Beyond quanMtaMve grading scores, addiMonal insights were obtained through ophthalmologist 
evaluaMon of model outputs. This evaluaMon idenMﬁed systemaMc semanMc misalignments in 
explanatory content that were not captured by predicMon accuracy alone. As illustrated in Figure 1, 
although OcularChat correctly idenMﬁed the absence of advanced AMD, its explanaMon emphasized 
drusen size and pigmentary abnormaliMes rather than the deﬁning features of advanced disease, i.e., 
geographic atrophy and neovascular disease. While accurate idenMﬁcaMon of all stages of AMD is 
clinically important, parMcularly for risk straMﬁcaMon and iniMaMon of AREDS2 supplementaMon, this 
pauern highlights a misalignment between the diagnosMc target and the explanatory focus. Speciﬁcally, 
conﬂaMng features of earlier disease stages with criteria for advanced AMD may obscure the disMncMon 
between disease severity categories, which is of clinical concern for neovascular AMD, where Mmely 
detecMon is criMcal given the availability of eﬀecMve vision-preserving therapies. These ﬁndings indicate 
that correct diagnosMc labels do not necessarily correspond to clinically valid or stage-appropriate 
reasoning. 
This issue was more evident in the reference model, whose verbose outputs frequently combined some 
correct conclusions with inaccurate or irrelevant anatomical descripMons, including references to regions 
not central to the diagnosMc task. Clinicians consistently noted that this response style obscured the 
model’s ﬁnal judgment. Although the reference model occasionally included appropriate guidance (e.g., 
recommending professional consultaMon or lifestyle modiﬁcaMon), it also increased suscepMbility to 
hallucinaMon and knowledge bias, which was reﬂected in consistently lower clinician scores for relevance 


13 
 
and internal consistency. In contrast, OcularChat produced concise, task-focused responses that reduced 
the likelihood of contradictory explanaMons and were perceived as beuer aligned with clinical workﬂows, 
parMcularly in opportunisMc screening scenarios where clear idenMﬁcaMon of pathologic ﬁndings is 
prioriMzed. In pracMce, OcularChat is intended to funcMon as a decision-support tool that complements 
clinician judgment by highlighMng salient image features and providing concise explanaMons, rather than 
replacing standard diagnosMc workﬂows. 
This work has several limitaMons. Although OcularChat’s more concise outputs were generally preferred 
for their eﬃciency and clarity, some ophthalmologists noted that highly simpliﬁed outputs insuﬃciently 
demonstrated image-grounded reasoning, raising concerns that predicMons parMally relied on learned 
priors rather than explicit visual evidence. This observaMon also reﬂects variability in clinician 
preferences, with some favoring concise, direcMve outputs and others valuing more detailed 
explanaMons to support exploratory reasoning or discussion.  
Another limitaMon is the reliance on CFPs, as it was trained exclusively on this single image modality. 
Although CFPs are central to reMnal evaluaMon, and reﬂect the reMnal appearance on clinical 
examinaMon, they do not always capture the full range of structural informaMon required for ophthalmic 
diagnosis in all semngs. OpMcal coherence tomography (OCT), in parMcular, provides high-resoluMon 3-
dimensional imaging, especially for the early diagnosis of the neovascular form of late AMD41-44. 
Nevertheless, CFPs remain highly advantageous for large-scale screening applicaMons, as they can be 
acquired using cost-eﬀecMve imaging devices, and are widely available across diverse clinical semngs. 
In summary, this study demonstrates the feasibility of adapMng MLLMs for reMnal image interpretaMon, 
with clinician evaluaMon supporMng their potenMal role as interpretable decision-support tools in AMD 
assessment, with scope for further expansion to broader ophthalmic applicaMons. By integraMng image-
based diagnosis with clinically grounded explanaMons and interacMve dialogue, OcularChat illustrates 


14 
 
how MLLMs can move beyond ﬁxed-output classiﬁcaMon toward supporMng real-world clinical reasoning 
and paMent communicaMon.  
Methods 
This main study used publicly available data from the AREDS35, a mulMcenter 12-year clinical trial 
conducted across 11 clinical sites in the United States. The original AREDS study was approved by the 
InsMtuMonal Review Board (IRB) at all parMcipaMng sites, and wriuen informed consent was obtained 
from all parMcipants. Eligible parMcipants underwent stereoscopic color fundus photography (CFP; 30° 
ﬁeld centered on the fovea) of both eyes at baseline and annually for up to 12 years of follow-up. 
ParMcipants were categorized into AMD severity groups, including individuals with no AMD. 
For the current study, CFPs and corresponding eye-level annotaMons (described below) were selected 
from the AREDS dataset. Data were split at the parMcipant level into training, validaMon, and test sets to 
prevent informaMon leakage, ensuring that images from the same parMcipant did not appear in other 
subsets. To ensure generalizability across eyes, images from both eyes were included. 
Dataset Construc#on and Dialogue Genera#on 
To ensure clinical relevance and contextual accuracy during model training, simulated paMent-physician 
dialogues were generated using key clinical variables extracted from the AREDS dataset. These variables 
included demographic characterisMcs (age, gender, diabetes status, and smoking history) and ophthalmic 
features (presence of advanced AMD, maximum drusen size, and presence of pigmentary abnormaliMes),

S. 1 Dataset Construction and Dialogue Generation 
In dialogue generation, a total of 705,850 patient-physician dialogues were generated through GPT-4V with 
temperature of 0.5 and 1024 maximum tokens. The generated dialogues, paired with their corresponding retinal 
images, formed the training dataset. Each sample consisted of a single pair of retinal images and associated 
dialogues formatted as alternating conversational turns. The generation strategy is shown in Figure S1. Retinal 
images were resized to 1024×1024 pixels and normalized following the pre-processing pipeline recommended for 
Qwen2.5-VL. No additional manual cropping or image enhancement was applied. 
 
S. 2 Training Details 
All parameters of Qwen2.5-VL-32B, including the vision and language encoders and the multilayer perceptron 
(MLP), were optimized during training. Training was conducted using Pytorch (version 2.6) in a distributed setting 
using eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs, each with 80 GB of memory and per-GPU batch size of 2. An effective batch size 
of 128 was achieved through gradient accumulation over eight steps. Mixed-precision training with bfloat16 (BF16) 
was utilized to enhance memory efficiency and computational performance. The learning rate was initialized at 1e-6 
and scheduled using cosine decay, with a warm-up phase comprising 3% of the total training steps to facilitate stable 
convergence. Optimization was performed using AdamW optimizer with default settings. The model was trained to 
minimize cross-entropy loss between predicted and target dialogue tokens, conditioned on both the fundus image 
and preceding conversational context. Model checkpoints were saved at regular intervals, and training was 
conducted for two epochs. Unless otherwise specified, all remaining hyperparameters followed the official 
recommendations for Qwen2.5-VL. 
 
S. 3 Evaluation of Model Accuracy 
To facilitate large-scale analysis, the model was instructed to return its outputs in a structured JSON format. To 
evaluate performance, these outputs were compared with the ground truth labels derived from previous reading 
center grading of the AREDS retinal images. Specifically, performance was assessed using accuracy and F1 score. 
All analyses were conducted using Python (version 3.10.18), NumPy (version 2.1.2) and scikit-learn (version 1.6.1). 
All models were evaluated using the same prompts and decoding parameters (including temperature and maximum 
token length) to ensure fair comparison.
